prime.problem: Your constrained pipeline reports 100% valid output, and still ships wrong orders. A grammar can only ask "is this allowed here?", never "is this true?", so a dashboard that counts valid outputs will hide exactly the errors that matter to the business.
prime.fits: Last card of part 1, and the distinction the whole course keeps returning to. The schema card defined what "valid" means; this card separates it from "correct" before you learn how grammars work, so you never mistake one for the other.
expect: schema-valid vs correct vs out of scope
the escape hatch (anyOf with an out-of-scope branch)
prime.goal: Design an extraction so that the model does only the reading, code does the arithmetic, and inputs that don't fit the schema have somewhere to go.

attend: Why does "total_usd": 60 pass a grammar exactly as easily as 54?
All 8 wrong grammar-on answers had the right items. What does that tell you about which part of the task the model got wrong?
Why does minItems: 1 turn a McFlurry request into a made-up order, and what does the escape hatch change?
Why can't the card claim the grammar made answers more correct, even though 22/30 beats 15/30?
For which kinds of fields does "compute it in code" not work, and what replaces it?

must: A grammar checks each token against the schema → 60 is a number just like 54 → wrong values are schema-valid → "30/30 valid" says nothing about how many are right
The model reads items and quantities well but adds badly → move the sum to code from your price list → 22/30 correct becomes 30/30, because every wrong answer had the right items
A strict schema has no way to say "not an order" → minItems: 1 forces at least one SKU → the model invents an order → add an out-of-scope branch so refusing is a valid output
n = 30 per arm → 22 vs 15 gives p ≈ 0.11 with overlapping ranges → the difference is a hint, not evidence that grammars make models smarter
elevated: An escape-hatch branch adds a second shape to the output → every consumer must handle it → and the provider must support anyOf, which hosted APIs don't always do
reference: the per-seed chip rows for all three setups
the escape-hatch JSON and prompt wording

compress.prompt: In three sentences, from memory: what a grammar guarantees, what it can't, and the two design moves that close most of the gap. Then name one kind of field where neither move works.
checklist: a grammar guarantees parse and schema validity, never truth
compute derived fields (totals, dates, lookups) in code
give out-of-scope inputs a valid place to go (an escape-hatch branch)
judgement fields (which product, sentiment) need an eval set, a second model or a person
30 runs can hint at a difference but can't prove one

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between schema-valid, correct and out of scope, using one output from the running example for each.
answer: schema-valid: parses and fits every keyword, e.g. total 60
correct: values match the input, total 54 = 3 × 12 + 1 × 18
out of scope: the input isn't an order at all ("I want a McFlurry"); the right output is a refusal the strict schema can't express

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens, token by token, when the grammar reaches "total_usd": and the model believes the total is 60.
answer: the grammar allows any number here
the digits 6 and 0 are allowed, so the mask removes nothing the model wanted
the output is valid, and only a value check that knows the prices can catch it

retrieve.q: Compare three ways to fix the 8 wrong totals: add a maximum, ask the model to double-check, or compute the total in code. Which do you pick, and what does each cost or miss?
answer: a maximum still lets 60 through, and JSON Schema can't express "equals the sum"
double-checking costs a second pass and can repeat or introduce errors (not tested)
computing in code fixes all 8 (22 + 8 = 30/30) at almost no cost, but only where a rule exists

compare.q: Computing the total in code and running a repair loop with a value check both target wrong values. What is fundamentally different, and when does each one win?
answer: computing replaces the model's value; the repair loop asks the model to try again
computing fixed 30/30 in one call; the repair loop reached 26/30 at 1.67 calls per request, with 4 stuck on 60 or 78
compute when a rule exists; repair when the check is possible but the value can't be computed (e.g. a lookup the model must choose)

compare.q: A wrong total of 60 and an engine that lets an empty items array through are both "bad output". Which one is a grammar failure, and which one no grammar could fix?
answer: the empty array is an under-constrained engine: it breaks the schema, so a correct grammar would block it
60 is schema-valid, so even a perfect grammar allows it
one is fixed by a better engine or a validator; the other only by a value check

predict.q: You rerun the 30 constrained calls at temperature 0 with no other change. Predict: does the correct count go to 30/30, stay near 22/30, or can't you tell?
predict.answer: You can't tell from the setup alone, but it will be either 0/30 or 30/30, because greedy decoding gives all 30 runs the same answer. The sampling card ran 3 greedy calls and got the right total every time, so for this prompt the greedy path happens to be correct. Temperature changes how often the model's wrong beliefs surface; it can't fix a model whose top guess is wrong.

apply.task: Write check(order, prices) that returns a list of problems: unknown SKU, qty below 1, and total not equal to the sum of qty × price. Run it on the 30 grammar-on totals from the card (22 × 54, 5 × 60, and one each of 58, 62, 66), with the items fixed at BW-CITRUS × 3 and CANDLE-LAVENDER × 1. Then write the escape-hatch schema and check that it accepts {"out_of_scope": "not an order"} and rejects {}.
apply.done: Your check flags exactly 8 of 30 with offsets +6 (×5), +4, +8 and +12, passes the other 22, and your anyOf schema accepts the out-of-scope object and rejects the empty one when validated with jsonschema.
apply.hint: The true total is 3 × 12 + 1 × 18 = 54. The out-of-scope branch needs required: ["out_of_scope"] or an empty object slips through.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: what temperature 0 does to the correct count?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the grammar can't catch 60, or why 22 vs 15 isn't proof?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: strict schema → invented order, or escape hatch → extra consumer work?
Which fields in your own schema could be computed instead of generated?
What will you look for later: where the course's "valid ≠ correct" line shows up again (masking, repair, coverage)?
